newsitem.title: ESTONIA: ESTONIA-PENNU AIMS AT 100 PERCENT GROWTH IN 97.
newsitem.headline: ESTONIA-PENNU AIMS AT 100 PERCENT GROWTH IN 97.

text.p: Pennu Computer, the only information technology (IT) company on a Baltic bourse, plans turnover growth of over 100 percent based on local and export sales, Lembit Abileid, managing director, said on Thursday.
"Our 1997 forecast is for 250 million kroons which is over 100 percent of our 1996 result of 121.3 million kroons," he told Reuters in an interview.
However, the company's growth in 1996 was only 85 percent and they are looking to export markets to maintain growth.
"We must expand to maintain our growth as the Estonian makret is too small," he added.
The company, which assembles computers and re-sells computer components, faces strong competion but is expecting an increasing share of the Estonian market.
"Last year we had 15-20 percent of the Estonian market and in 1997 we are aiming for 25 percent," Abileid said.
"By the end of the year we expect to sell about 600-700 units a month in Estonia with the local market for new computers growing from 25,000 in 1996 to 35,000 in 1997."
The company is looking to take advange of Estonia's trade agreements with Finland to give it an edge over Finnish assemblers and Asian exporters.
"We hope to be selling 200 units a month to Finland by the end of the year," he said.
"Estonia's agreement with Finland gave Estonia a tariff of only two percent when importing products to Finalnd and companies from Asia have four percent."
"Our costs are 20-25 percent lower than local Finnish companies and this give us an advantage," he added.
The company is already selling 100 units a week to Latvia through a local partner and the company is aiming at sales of 200 units a month to Latvia as well.
"We are not opening representative offices in Latvia and Lithuania but we are seeking partners, who know local needs and local markets," he said.
"We have a new partner in Lithuania and the cooperation seems to be working," Abileid added.
To fill the demand, the company's assembly plant can produce 2000 units a month but it is currently only producing about 500 units with a planned year end production of 1000 units a month.
The company, like most IT firms, is affected by the U.S. exchange rate as they buy components and export in dollars.
Abileid said their competitors face the some issue so he felt that the company was not at a disadvantage.
